title: Probability refresh | Modern data tooling
objectives: Re-derive core probability results at interview speed. Set up a local analytics stack (DuckDB, Polars, dbt) you will reuse all quarter.
exercise: Download a public transactions or rides dataset. Load it into DuckDB, build two dbt models (staging → daily metrics) with unique and not_null tests, and compute the same daily metric in Polars to cross-check.
resources: Harvard Stat 110 (Joe Blitzstein): lecture videos free
Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed. (free at probabilitybook.net)

units.title: Conditional probability & Bayes
units.concepts: Conditional probability, Bayes' rule, independence, base rates

units.title: Why columnar & Parquet
units.concepts: Row vs column storage, compression, row groups, predicate pushdown

units.title: DuckDB basics
units.concepts: In-process OLAP, querying files directly, Arrow interop

units.title: Expectation tricks & CLT
units.concepts: Linearity of expectation, indicators, LLN, CLT, classic puzzles

cards.q: A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific, and prevalence is 1%. What is P(disease | positive)? Answer in %.
Which is Bayes' rule?
cards.explain: Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.

cards.q: Events A and B are independent exactly when…
cards.explain: Equivalently P(A|B) = P(A). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probability are actually dependent.

cards.q: A family has two children. At least one is a boy. What is the probability both are boys? (decimal)
cards.explain: Sample space {BB, BG, GB}, equally likely. Only BB qualifies: 1/3.

cards.q: Why is P(disease | positive) so low for a 99%-sensitive test on a rare disease?
choices: False positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives from the small sick group
The test is not independent of the disease
cards.explain: Base-rate effect: 5% of 99% healthy people dwarfs 99% of 1% sick people.

cards.q: Which distribution models the number of fraud alerts per hour, and what are its mean and variance?
cards.answer: Poisson(λ): counts of independent events in a fixed interval at a constant rate. Mean = variance = λ.
rubric: Bonus: notes overdispersion (variance > mean) suggests negative binomial, e.g. fraud bursts

cards.q: Variance of a Binomial(n, p)?
cards.explain: Sum of n independent Bernoulli(p), each with variance p(1−p). p(1−p)/n is the variance of the sample proportion.

cards.q: Each loan application is approved with p = 0.2, independently. Expected number of applications until the first approval (including it)?
cards.explain: Geometric (trials until first success): mean 1/p = 5.

cards.q: Alerts arrive as Poisson with λ = 2 per hour. P(no alerts in an hour)? (decimal, 3 dp)
When is Poisson(np) a good approximation to Binomial(n, p)?
cards.explain: Law of rare events: many trials, each unlikely.

cards.q: Why is the exponential distribution memoryless, and when does that assumption fail for ride wait times?
cards.answer: P(T > s+t | T > s) = e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs) = e^(−λt) = P(T > t): constant hazard, so time already waited carries no information. It fails when the hazard changes over time: a driver already en route (wait shrinks), surge or shift changes, scheduled pickups, or bunched supply.
rubric: Shows the survival-function ratio or says 'constant hazard rate'
Gives a realistic reason the hazard is not constant for ride waits

cards.q: Mean of an Exponential with rate λ?
cards.explain: Mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ². ln2/λ is the median.

cards.q: What percentage of a standard normal lies within ±1.96?
cards.explain: This is where the 1.96 in 95% confidence intervals comes from.

cards.q: Wait time is exponential with mean 4 minutes. You've already waited 3 minutes. Expected additional wait (minutes)?
cards.explain: Memorylessness: the remaining wait has the same distribution as a fresh wait, mean 4.

cards.q: Which is the only memoryless continuous distribution?
cards.explain: The geometric is its discrete counterpart.

cards.q: Expected number of rolls of a fair die until you get a 6?
cards.explain: Geometric with p = 1/6, mean 1/p = 6.

cards.q: Why does the CLT justify a z-test on mean revenue per user?
cards.answer: The sample mean of many i.i.d. users is approximately normal, whatever the shape of revenue per user, with SE = σ/√n. So a z-statistic on the difference in means is approximately standard normal. Caveat: revenue is heavy-tailed, so convergence is slow. You need large n, or capping/winsorising.
rubric: Sample mean approximately normal regardless of the underlying distribution
Mentions heavy tails / skew slow convergence

cards.q: Coupon collector: expected rolls of a fair die to see all 6 faces? (1 dp)
Birthday problem: with 23 people (365 equally likely days), P(at least two share a birthday)? Answer in %.
A random permutation of 10 cards: expected number of cards that end up in their original position?
cards.explain: Indicator trick: each card is fixed with probability 1/10; 10 × 1/10 = 1, whatever the dependence between cards.

cards.q: Linearity of expectation E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] requires…
choices: Nothing beyond finite expectations: no independence needed
cards.explain: That's why indicator tricks work on dependent events.

cards.q: Why does a columnar format speed up SELECT avg(amount) but not single-row lookups?
cards.answer: Columnar storage keeps each column contiguous. An aggregate reads only the 'amount' column, which compresses well and supports vectorised scanning. A single-row lookup needs every column of one row, which means touching many separate column chunks, so row stores (with indexes) win there.
rubric: Aggregate reads only needed columns (less I/O)
Row lookup must stitch values from every column

cards.q: What lets a Parquet reader skip whole row groups for WHERE txn_date = '2026-01-05'?
choices: Min/max statistics stored per column chunk (predicate pushdown)
cards.explain: If the filter value falls outside a row group's min/max, the reader skips that group.

cards.q: Why do columns compress better than rows?
choices: Values in one column share a type and repeat, so dictionary/RLE encodings work well

cards.q: Which workload is a row-oriented (OLTP) store better suited to?
choices: Many small inserts/updates of whole records

cards.q: 'Projection pushdown' means…
choices: Reading only the columns the query uses

cards.q: Can DuckDB query a Polars DataFrame without copying it? What enables that?
choices: Yes: both use the Apache Arrow columnar memory format
No, it must be exported to CSV first
cards.explain: Arrow's shared memory layout allows zero-copy hand-off.

cards.q: DuckDB is best described as…
choices: An in-process analytical (OLAP) database, like 'SQLite for analytics'

cards.q: How do you query a Parquet file in DuckDB without loading it into a table first?
Where is DuckDB a poor fit?
choices: Backend for a high-concurrency web app with many simultaneous writers
Ad-hoc analysis of a 20 GB Parquet file on a laptop

cards.q: Give two reasons DuckDB can beat pandas on a 20 GB Parquet dataset on a laptop.
cards.answer: Vectorised, multi-threaded execution; out-of-core processing that spills to disk, so it doesn't need everything in RAM; projection/predicate pushdown so it reads only needed columns and row groups; a query optimiser.
rubric: Any two of: multi-threaded vectorised engine, larger-than-memory/spilling, pushdown, query optimiser

cards.q: What does scan_parquet do differently from read_parquet in Polars?
choices: Returns a LazyFrame: builds a query plan and reads only what's needed on collect()
Reads the file faster but eagerly
cards.explain: Lazy mode lets the optimiser push projections and filters into the scan.

cards.q: What triggers execution of a Polars LazyFrame?
Why are Polars expressions (pl.col('x') * 2) faster than a Python UDF via map_elements?
choices: Expressions run vectorised and in parallel in Rust; UDFs call Python row by row

cards.q: Which optimisation can the lazy engine apply that eager mode cannot?
choices: Predicate pushdown into the file scan

cards.q: How would you inspect the optimised plan of a LazyFrame?
Name two built-in dbt tests and what they guard against.
cards.answer: unique (duplicate keys), not_null (missing values), accepted_values (unexpected categories), relationships (orphan foreign keys, i.e. referential integrity).
rubric: Any two of unique / not_null / accepted_values / relationships

cards.q: What does {{ ref('stg_rides') }} do in a dbt model?
choices: Resolves the right table name and records a dependency edge in the DAG

cards.q: A dbt model is fundamentally…
choices: A SELECT statement that dbt materialises as a view/table in the warehouse

Which dbt test catches transactions whose merchant_id doesn't exist in dim_merchants?
